title: 12-1 Speeding Stops
text:
Introduction
In my analysis, I work with tables containing data on traffic stops made by state patrols in Rhode Island, North Carolina, and Massachusetts. Specifically, I examine whether there are differences across states in the proportion of arrests made during traffic stops with speeding as the stated reason for the stop. I consider the time period from 2007 to 2015, as the data tables overlap over this time frame. I have hidden the output of the queries below, as they are useful if one wants to visualize the contents of each data table but don’t involve any important wrangling. I hypothesize that Rhode Island has a higher proportion of arrests made for speeding stops than the two other states given its higher population density, which I infer makes for stricter speeding laws. I expect the difference to be smaller between Rhode Island and Massachusetts, given that the difference in their population density is very small.

title: 12-1 Speeding Stops
text:
Data Wrangling
In the SQL query below, I calculate the yearly arrest percentages for traffic stops due to speeding in each state and join the results to create a data table with state-year pair observations. Storing the output table as an object in R allows me to use it later on for data visualization and statistical tests. Below is a preview of what the table looks like.


Show the code
SELECT
  'RI' AS state,
  YEAR(`date`) AS year,
  COUNT(*) AS total_stops,
  SUM(arrest_made) AS arrests,
  (SUM(arrest_made) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS arrest_percentage
FROM ri_statewide_2020_04_01
WHERE reason_for_stop = 'Speeding' 
AND YEAR(`date`) BETWEEN 2007 AND 2015
GROUP BY YEAR(`date`)

UNION ALL

SELECT
  'NC' AS state,
  YEAR(`date`) AS year,
  COUNT(*) AS total_stops,
  SUM(arrest_made) AS arrests,
  (SUM(arrest_made) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS arrest_percentage
FROM nc_statewide_2020_04_01
WHERE reason_for_stop = 'Speed Limit Violation'
AND YEAR(`date`) BETWEEN 2007 AND 2015
GROUP BY YEAR(`date`)

UNION ALL

SELECT
  'MA' AS state,
  YEAR(STR_TO_DATE(`date`, '%Y-%m-%d')) AS year,
  COUNT(*) AS total_stops,
  SUM(arrest_made) AS arrests,
  (SUM(arrest_made) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS arrest_percentage
FROM ma_statewide_2020_04_01
WHERE reason_for_stop = 'Speed'
AND YEAR(`date`) BETWEEN 2007 AND 2015
GROUP BY YEAR(STR_TO_DATE(`date`, '%Y-%m-%d'))

ORDER BY state, year;

title: 12-1 Speeding Stops
text:
Plot #1


Show the code
state_colors <- c("RI" = "#E41A1C", "NC" = "#377EB8", "MA" = "#4DAF4A")

ggplot(stops_table, aes(x = year, y = arrest_percentage, color = state, group = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = state_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Arrests for Speeding Stops by State Over Time",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Arrest Percentage (%)",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The above plot portrays the time series trend of arrest percentages for speeding-induced traffic stops in each respective state. It is interesting to note that North Carolina has higher consistency in arrest percentage over time than the other two states, who both trend downwards. This could signal that certain policies were enacted that reduced the chance of a speeding offense leading to arrest, such as more lenient regulations.

title: 12-1 Speeding Stops
text:
Plot #2
Test: RI vs MA

Null hypothesis (H₀): RI’s mean arrest percentage is less than or equal to MA’s
Alternative hypothesis (H₁): RI’s mean arrest percentage is greater than MA’s
Testing whether Rhode Island has a statistically significantly higher average arrest percentage for speeding stops compared to Massachusetts over the 2007-2015 period



Show the code
ri_arrests <- stops_table |>
  filter(state == "RI") |> pull(arrest_percentage)
   ma_arrests <- stops_table |>
     filter(state == "MA") |>
     pull(arrest_percentage)
   nc_arrests <- stops_table |>
     filter(state == "NC") |>
     pull(arrest_percentage)
   
p_ri_ma <- t.test(ri_arrests, ma_arrests, alternative = "greater")$p.value
p_ri_nc <- t.test(ri_arrests, nc_arrests, alternative = "greater")$p.value

y_min <- 0.70
y_max <- 1.50

stops_table |>
  filter(state %in% c("RI", "MA")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = arrest_percentage, fill = state)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = y_max * 0.95, 
           label = paste0("p = ", round(p_ri_ma, 4)), 
           size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "RI vs MA: Arrest Percentages for Speeding Stops (2007-2015)",
    x = "State",
    y = "Arrest Percentage (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("MA" = "#4DAF4A", "RI" = "#E41A1C")) +
  ylim(y_min, y_max)









The above plot showcases the difference in arrest percentages between Rhode Island and Massachusetts, with RI higher than MA. However, the p-value is greater than 0.05 which means the difference is not statistically significant, perhaps because the population densities of both states are extremely similar. We cannot reject the null hypothesis.

title: 12-1 Speeding Stops
text:
Plot #3
Test: RI vs NC

Null hypothesis (H₀): RI’s mean arrest percentage is less than or equal to NC’s
Alternative hypothesis (H₁): RI’s mean arrest percentage is greater than NC’s
Testing whether Rhode Island has a statistically significantly higher average arrest percentage for speeding stops compared to North Carolina over the 2007-2015 period



Show the code
stops_table |>
  filter(state %in% c("RI", "NC")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = arrest_percentage, fill = state)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = y_max * 0.95, 
           label = paste0("p = ", round(p_ri_nc, 4)), 
           size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "RI vs NC: Arrest Percentages for Speeding Stops (2007-2015)",
    x = "State",
    y = "Arrest Percentage (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("NC" = "#377EB8", "RI" = "#E41A1C")) +
  ylim(y_min, y_max)









Based on the above plot, we can see that Rhode Island has a statistically significant higher proportion of arrests for speeding-induced traffic stops than North Carolina. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis. It is possible that North Carolina’s much smaller population density (around 1/5) has prompted less serious penalties for speeding in the state.

title: 12-1 Speeding Stops
text:
Conclusion:
In summary, I was able to reject the null hypothesis in one of the two tests conducted, with the difference between RI and NC being statistically significant. Although analysis across a larger group of high density vs low density states would be beneficial, it is difficult to conduct using this set of databases because state patrols have different ways of classifying reasons for stops. In fact, for some there is no clear “speeding” category, and the stated reason is simply moving violation (which encompasses a wide range of reasons).

title: 10-28 Animal Shelter
text:
Sources linked:
 City of Long Beach Data 
 Tidy Tuesday Data


Show the code
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(gt)

shelter_data <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-04/longbeach.csv')



Research Plan:

My plan is to process the City of Long Beach animal shelter data from 2017 to 2025 to determine if people tend to adopt dogs more than cats. This is interesting to observe because it could lead us to infer that people have a preference for adopting one pet over the other, which has a plethora of potential explanations rooted in cognitive science.
Q: Are dogs adopted more often than cats?
Observational unit - Individual animals (cats and dogs) in the shelter.
Statistic (sample proportion) - Proportion of cats and proportion of dogs in the shelter that are adopted.
Parameter (population proportion) - True proportion of cats and true proportion of dogs in the shelter population that are adopted.
Variables - Choice of dog or cat (categorical) and Adopted or not (categorical).
Null Hypothesis - H₀: There is no difference in the proportion of dogs adopted and cats adopted.
Alternative Hypothesis - H₁: The proportion of dogs adopted is greater than the proportion of cats adopted.


Show the code
adoption_rates <- shelter_data |>
  filter(animal_type == "dog" | animal_type == "cat") |>
  mutate(Species = animal_type) |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  mutate(adopted = if_else(outcome_type == "adoption", 1, 0)) |>
  summarise("Adoption Rate" = mean(adopted, na.rm = TRUE))

observed_diff <- adoption_rates |>
  pull("Adoption Rate") |>
  diff()

adoption_rates |> gt()








Species
Adoption Rate




cat
0.2444523


dog
0.2661265







The above table highlights the observed proportions of adopted dogs and adopted cats. Approximately 24.4% of cats were adopted at the shelter, compared to 26.6% of dogs. This means the observed difference sits at 2.17%, meaning people in the sample adopted dogs at a rate 2.17% higher than the rate at which they adopted cats. Now, I will test whether this difference is statistically significant by conducting a permutation test over 1,000 iterations.


Show the code
not_summarized <- shelter_data |>
  filter(animal_type == "dog" | animal_type == "cat") |>
  mutate(Species = animal_type) |>
  mutate(adopted = if_else(outcome_type == "adoption", 1, 0))

permutation_test <- function(data) {
  data <- data |>
    mutate(adopted = sample(adopted, replace = FALSE)) |>
    group_by(Species) |>
    summarise(adopt_rate = mean(adopted, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    arrange(Species) |>
    pull(adopt_rate) |>
    diff()
}

set.seed(47)
null_diffs <- map_dbl(1:10000, ~ permutation_test(not_summarized))

p_value <- mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(observed_diff))


The permutation_test function:

Takes the original dataset.
Randomly shuffles the adopted column (breaking any link between species and adoption status).
Recalculates the adoption rates for dogs and cats.
Returns the difference in adoption rates (dog_rate - cat_rate) for that shuffled dataset.

By running this function 1,000 times using map_dbl(), I generate a distribution of differences that would occur if the null hypothesis were true.


Show the code
tibble(null_diffs = null_diffs) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = null_diffs)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_diff, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Null Distribution of Adoption Rate Differences (Dog - Cat)",
    subtitle = paste("1000 Iterations - ", "Observed difference:", round(observed_diff, 3), "| p-value:", p_value),
    x = "Difference in Adoption Rate",
    y = "Frequency"
  )










Plot Description:

The above plot is a visualization of the null distribution obtained from the permutation test based on 1,000 iterations. It shows us that it is extremely unlikely that the observed difference in adoption rates at the Long Beach animal shelter (2.2%) could occur if the null hypothesis were true. Therefore, I reject the null hypothesis because the p-value is nearly equal to 0 so the observed difference is statistically significant. The histogram shows the range of differences we would expect if the null hypothesis were true. This suggests that dogs are more likely to be adopted than cats in shelters. Animal shelters could use this insight to investigate why this might be occurring (marketing, pet descriptions, position of pets in the shelter, etc.).

country_lists <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-09-09/country_lists.csv')

Show the code
travel_perms <- country_lists |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(visa_required, visa_online, visa_on_arrival, 
             visa_free_access, electronic_travel_authorisation),
    names_to = "visa_type",
    values_to = "json_str"
 ) |> 
  mutate(
    json_parsed = map(json_str, ~ fromJSON(.)[[1]])
) |> 
  unnest(json_parsed, names_sep = "_") |> 
  select(-json_str) |> 
  rename(from = code, from_name = country,
         to = json_parsed_code, to_name = json_parsed_name) |> 
  mutate(from = ifelse(from_name == "Namibia", "NA", from)) 

# adding the home countries so that they show up on the map

  select(from, from_name) |> 
  distinct() |> 
  mutate(visa_type = "domestic",
         to = from,
         to_name = from_name)
travel_perms <- travel_perms |> rbind(home_countries)

world <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

world_data <- world |> 
  left_join(travel_perms, by = c("iso_a2_eh" = "to"))




Show the code

title: 10-5 Netflix
text:
Sources linked:
 Shivam Bansal - Kaggle Data 
 Tidy Tuesday Data


Show the code
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(gt)

Netflix_data <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-04-20/netflix_titles.csv')



Analysis #1: What is the breakdown (in % terms) of ratings for productions based on their main listed genre on Netflix?


Genres:

Listed Alphabetically

Action & Adventure: Action & Adventure + TV Action & Adventure
Anime: Anime Series
Children & Family: Children & Family Movies + Kids’ TV
Classics, Cult, & Musicals: Classic & Cult TV + Classic Movies + Cult Movies + Music & Musicals
Comedy & Drama: Comedies + Stand-up Comedy + TV Comedies + Dramas + TV Dramas
Crime: Crime TV Shows
Documentaries: Documentaries + Docuseries
Horror & Thriller: Horror Movies + Thrillers + TV Horror
Int’l & Independent: British TV Shows + International TV shows + International Movies + Independent Movies
Reality: Reality TV
Romance: Romantic Movies + Romantic TV Shows
Sci-Fi & Fantasy: Sci-Fi & Fantasy


Ratings:

Ordered from widest to smallest recommended audience

Y: TV-Y
Y7 & FV: TV-Y7 + TV-7Y-FV
G: G + TV-G
PG: PG + TV-PG
PG 13 & TV 14: PG-13 + TV-14
R & MA: R + TV-MA + NC-17
Other: NR + UR + NA



Show the code
Genre_Ratings <- Netflix_data |>
  mutate(
    First_Genre = str_extract(listed_in, "^[^,]+"),
    Genre = case_when(
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Action|Adventure|TV Action") ~ "Action & Adventure",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Anime") ~ "Anime",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Children|Kids'|Family") ~ "Children & Family",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Classic|Cult|Musical") ~ "Classics, Cult, & Musicals",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Comedy|Stand-up|Drama") ~ "Comedy & Drama",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Crime") ~ "Crime",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Documentaries|Docuseries") ~ "Documentaries",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Horror|Thriller") ~ "Horror & Thriller",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "British|International|Independent") ~ "Int'l & Independent",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Reality") ~ "Reality",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Romantic") ~ "Romance",
      str_detect(First_Genre, "Sci-Fi|Fantasy") ~ "Sci-Fi & Fantasy",
      TRUE ~ "Other")) |>
  filter(Genre != "Other") |>
  mutate( rating_ordered = case_when(
      str_detect(rating, "^TV-Y$") ~ "Y",
      str_detect(rating, "^(TV-Y7|TV-7Y-FV)$") ~ "Y7 & FV",
      str_detect(rating, "^(G$|^TV-G)$") ~ "G",
      str_detect(rating, "^(PG$|^TV-PG)$") ~ "PG",
      str_detect(rating, "^(PG-13$|^TV-14)$") ~ "PG 13 & TV 14",
      str_detect(rating, "^(R$|^TV-MA$|^NC-17)$") ~ "R & MA",
      str_detect(rating, "^(NR$|^UR$|^NA)$") | is.na(rating) ~ "Other")) |>
  select(title, rating, listed_in, Genre, rating_ordered)




Show the code
Ratings_Breakdown <- Genre_Ratings |>
   count(Genre, rating_ordered) |>
  group_by(Genre) |>
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100, rating_ordered = factor(
      rating_ordered,
      levels = c("Y", "Y7 & FV", "G", "PG", "PG 13 & TV 14", "R & MA", "Other"))) 




Show the code
Ratings_Breakdown |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rating_ordered, y = percentage, fill = rating_ordered)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~Genre) +
  labs(
    title = "Rating Distribution by Genre",
    subtitle = "Proportion (%)",
    x = "Rating Group",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Rating") + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100)) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(size = 6, face = "bold"), 
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"))










Plot description:

The above plot displays the distribution of ratings based on the genre of a production that can be found on Netflix. Some genres overwhelmingly fit under a single rating. For example, the Comedy & Drama genre is mostly rated R & MA, with a similar but more marked trend in the Crime genre and Horror & Thriller genre. These three all have one rating category making up 60%+ of their respective genre’s production. On the other hand, four genres are particularly balanced in their ratings split. The Children & Family genre, Classic, Cult, & Musicals genre, Reality genre, and the Documentaries genre all have at least three rating categories with a 20%+ share of their respective genre’s productions. The other 5 genres fall somewhere in between these two groups.

Analysis #2 What is geographical split of production locations for titles added to Netflix in 2019 compared to those added in 2020?



Show the code
Geo_Data <- Netflix_data |>
  mutate(year_added = as.numeric(str_sub(date_added, -4, -1)),
    countries = str_split(country, ", ")) |>
  select(year_added, country, countries) |>
  filter(year_added == 2019 | year_added == 2020) |>
  unnest(cols = countries) |>
  count(countries, year_added, name = "n_titles") |>
  mutate(
    bin = case_when(
      n_titles == 0 ~ "0",
      n_titles <= 2 ~ "1-2",
      n_titles <= 5 ~ "3-5",
      n_titles <= 10 ~ "6-10",
      n_titles <= 25 ~ "11-25",
      TRUE ~ "25+"
    )) |>
   mutate(
    countries = case_when(
      countries == "German Democratic Republic" ~ "Germany",
      countries == "Hong Kong SAR China" ~ "Hong Kong",
      countries == "United States" ~ "United States of America",
      countries == "Vatican City" ~ "Holy See",
      TRUE ~ countries
    ))




Show the code
world <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

map_data_2019 <- world |>
  left_join(Geo_Data |>    
  filter(year_added == 2019)|>
      mutate(
        n_titles = ifelse(is.na(n_titles), 0, n_titles),
        bin = factor(bin, levels = c("0", "1-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-25", "25+"))
      ),
    by = c("name" = "countries"))

map_data_2020 <- world |> 
  left_join(Geo_Data |> 
  filter(year_added == 2020)|>
      mutate(
        n_titles = ifelse(is.na(n_titles), 0, n_titles),
        bin = factor(bin, levels = c("0", "1-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-25", "25+"))
      ),
    by = c("name" = "countries"))

p2019 <- ggplot(map_data_2019) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = bin, text = paste0(name, ": ", n_titles, " titles")), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("1-2" = "lightblue", "3-5" = "turquoise", "6-10" = "royalblue", "11-25" = "blue", "25+" = "navyblue"),
    labels = c("1-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-25", "25+", "0"),
    na.value = "grey"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Netflix Productions by Country (2019)",
    fill = "Number of Titles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot_2019 <- ggplotly(p2019, tooltip = "text")

p2020 <- ggplot(map_data_2020) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = bin, text = paste0(name, ": ", n_titles, " titles")), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("1-2" = "lightblue", "3-5" = "turquoise", "6-10" = "royalblue", "11-25" = "blue", "25+" = "navyblue"),
    labels = c("1-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-25", "25+", "0"),
    na.value = "grey"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Netflix Productions by Country (2020)",
    fill = "Number of Titles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot_2020 <- ggplotly(p2020, tooltip = "text")


plot_2019






Show the code
plot_2020







Plot Description:

The above maps display ranges for the number of titles added to Netflix by the country in which they were produced. By hovering your cursor over a country, you can identify the specific number of titles added. The comparison between 2019 and 2020 allows us to see which countries saw more of their productions added to the platform year over year. Focusing on North American countries, we see some interesting changes. While most productions added were in the US during both years, the number actually declined from 2019 to 2020, declining from 926 to 888 titles. Canada saw an increase from 91 to 115 titles. Finally, Mexico saw a decline from 41 to 32 titles. By conducting a broader time series analysis, we could make inferences about how some countries become more favorable production environments over time (which increases the number of titles produced in that country Netflix adds). Another explanation could be that as Netflix attempts to reach wider audiences, they diversify the titles that they offer on their streaming platform. A time series analysis could provide insight on Netflix’s changing global content strategy.

Analysis #3 What is the average title length based on a production’s type (show vs movie)? Do movie titles contain more descriptive phrases (like “The [X] of [Y]”) compared to TV show titles



Show the code
title_patterns <- Netflix_data |>
  mutate( has_descriptive_phrase = str_detect(title, "(?i)(^| )(the|a|an) [a-z]+ of [a-z]+($| )"), word_count = str_count(title, "\\w+")) |>
  group_by(type) |>
  summarize(avg_title_length = mean(str_length(title)),
    pct_desc_phrases = mean(has_descriptive_phrase) * 100, total_titles = n()) |>
  mutate("Type" = type, "Avg Title Length" = avg_title_length, "% w/ desc phrases" = pct_desc_phrases, "Total Titles" = total_titles) |>
  select("Type", "Avg Title Length", "% w/ desc phrases", "Total Titles") |>

title: 11-11 Poorly Anonymized Data
text:
Article Sources:
Johnston, Anna. “Bradley Cooper’s Taxi Ride: A Lesson in Privacy Risk.” Helios Salinger, 19 April 2015, https://www.heliossalinger.com.au/2015/04/19/bradley-coopers-taxi-ride-a-lesson-in-privacy-risk/
Goodin, Dan. “Poorly Anonymized Logs Reveal NYC Cab Drivers’ Detailed Whereabouts.” Ars Technica, 23 June 2014,  https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2014/06/poorly-anonymized-logs-reveal-nyc-cab-drivers-detailed-whereabouts/

Analysis of the TLC Taxi Data’s Ethical Controversy

Were the data made publicly available? Why? How? On what platform?
What was the consent structure for recruiting participants?

In 2014, the New York City Taxi & Limousine commission released, under FOI, data recorded by taxis’ GPS systems, with the data set covering over 173 million individual trips taken during 2013. “Under FOI” means government records are being made public in response to a request under the Freedom of Information Act, so the first element of importance is that this information was accessible to anyone. The data set was published on the NYC government website. According to Johnston, each trip record in the data included the “date, location and time of the pickup and drop-off, the fare paid, and any recorded tip…it also included a unique code for each taxi and taxi driver”. The taxi drivers and passengers did not explicitly consent to the release of ride data by the TLC in 2014, so the government attempted to make their identities anonymous in order to avoid them from being identified.

Is the data identifiable? Is anonymity guaranteed?

Unfortunately, city officials failed to guarantee anonymity. Goodin explains that officials used cryptographic hashes to obscure drivers’ hack license numbers and medallion numbers, using the MD5 algorithm to preserve the privacy of individual drivers. However, drivers’ hack and medallion numbers are structured predictably (taxi license numbers are always 6 or 7 digit numbers that start with a 5) so there were only 2 million possible license combinations. Goodin states that “Software developer Vijay…in less than two hours…had completely de-anonymized all 173 million entries”. City officials poorly anonymized the data by choosing an encryption option that was not appropriate for the data structure since license and medallion numbers come in predictable patterns. Information on which driver took every single trip was now identifiable, as were the aforementioned details of said trips. From another angle, Johnston mentions that “even if TLC had removed all the details about the driver and the taxi, the geolocation data alone could potentially identify taxi passengers”.

Is the data being used in unintended ways to the original study?

According to Johnston, the data was initially meant to be used for “urban transport and planning research”. However, the poor anonymisation of drivers’ identities meant that anyone could now figure out in less than 2 hours which driver drove every single trip in the data set, and subsequently calculate drivers’ income, infer where they live, know how many miles they drove, or find out where they were at any given time. In addition, taxi passengers could be identified based on geolocation regardless of if the data was anonymous. Johnston points out that when Anthony Tockar googled images of celebrities getting in or out of taxis in 2013 coupled with data from celebrity gossip blogs, he was able to determine where and when celebrities got into taxis. Given this information, he was able to identify where Bradley Cooper went and how much he paid for each ride, which led to public backlash for his poor track record with tipping. Cooper’s PR team defended him by arguing that cash tips were not recorded in the data set - but by that point, the damage had been done and his privacy was infringed on.

Who benefits? Who is neglected or harmed?

In sum, poor data anonymization made possible the identification of taxi drivers’ ride information and the identification of passengers based on geolocation data alone. While the Bradley Cooper example reflects a relatively minor breach of privacy, Johnston remarks that the same process could be used to easily identify the start or end-point for each taxi trip to or from an abortion clinic, a drug counselling service, or the home address of an investigative journalist or suspected whistle-blower. The ethical violations, though not intentional, reflect neglect of personal privacy for both taxi drivers and passengers, serving the interest of surveillance. The people who benefit are malintentioned individuals intending to track others’ movement in New York City, while harming the privacy of drivers and passengers alike. While data transparency on taxi movements and the intent to de-identify driver data were well-meaning, the consequences of poorly anonymized data end up causing more harm than good. The poorly anonymized data is a violation of the data values and principles manifesto, especially the principle to “protect the privacy and security of individuals represented in our data.” This case reflects broader themes in Data Feminism: data science tends to be prioritized for transparency and efficiency but often overlooks the populations harmed in the process.
